title: The Ancient Near East
tagline: From the city-states of Sumer to Persia: two thousand years of Near Eastern kingdoms and empires.
intro: Some of the oldest known law codes and what is widely regarded as the first empire arose in Mesopotamia and the lands around it, from southwestern Iran to Anatolia and the Lebanese coast. The path starts in Lagash, a Sumerian city-state, and follows the powers that rose over the region in turn: Akkad, the Third Dynasty of Ur, Elam, Babylon, the Hittites and Assyria. Urartu in the mountains and the Phoenician cities on the coast lived beside them, and the Achaemenid Persians, who entered Babylon in 539 BCE, gathered most of these lands into one empire.

steps.why: A Sumerian city-state whose Stele of the Vultures records Eannatum's victory over Umma around 2450 BCE, and whose ruler Urukagina made reforms that may be the first legal code.
Sargon of Akkad brought the city-states of Sumer and Akkad under one ruler around 2334 BCE, in what is widely regarded as the world's first empire.
After the Akkadian collapse the Third Dynasty of Ur revived Sumerian rule, kept tens of thousands of tablets and issued the oldest law code that survives.
From Susa and Anshan in southwestern Iran, Elam sacked Ur around 2004 BCE, carried off its last king, Ibbi-Sin, and later overthrew the Kassite dynasty of Babylon.
Under Hammurabi a small Amorite city-state mastered Mesopotamia in barely a decade, and his Code of 282 laws is the fullest to survive from the ancient Near East.
Ruled from Hattusa in Anatolia, the Hittites raided Babylon around 1595 BCE, fought Egypt at Kadesh in 1274 BCE and later concluded a peace treaty with Ramesses II.
From the city of Assur, Assyria grew into the largest empire yet seen, reaching Egypt in 671 BCE, until Medes and Babylonians destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE.
Assyria's great northern rival, a mountain kingdom around Lake Van whose kings built rock fortresses and canals; Argishti I founded Erebuni, the origin of Yerevan, in 782 BCE.
Rival city-states of the Lebanese coast such as Tyre, Sidon and Byblos, which sold cedar and purple cloth and whose ships formed the core of the Persian navy after 539 BCE.
Cyrus the Great entered Babylon in 539 BCE, and the empire he built stretched from the Indus to the Aegean and the Nile until Alexander the Great conquered it.

title: Languages and Their Peoples
tagline: Ten languages and the peoples, cities and empires that spoke, wrote and carried them.
intro: A language travels with the people who speak it and the states that use it. This path follows ten of them, roughly in order of age, from Sumerian, first written at Uruk around 3200 BCE, to Swahili, which grew in the merchant towns of the East African coast. Some, such as Sumerian, Latin and Ge'ez, outlived their speakers as written languages of learning, law or worship. Others, such as Arabic, Nahuatl and Swahili, became common languages of faith, empire or trade far beyond the lands where they began.

steps.why: The language of the city-states of southern Mesopotamia, whose speakers developed cuneiform around 3200 BCE; it stayed a language of learning long after it ceased to be spoken.
The oldest recorded Semitic language, spoken in the empires of Akkad, Babylon and Assyria, and in the Amarna letters the language of diplomacy between Egypt and its neighbours.
First known from the hymns of the Rigveda, composed in the north-west of the subcontinent around 1500–1200 BCE, and codified by Panini in some four thousand rules.
The written language of Confucius and the historians of ancient China, rooted in Shang oracle bones and used for government in Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
The language of Latium and Rome, which spread with Roman power and changed region by region into Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and Romanian.
First recorded in inscriptions of the Arabian peninsula and its desert borderlands, it became a world language with the Qur'an and the conquests of the 7th century.
The language of the Kingdom of Aksum, carved on stone from the 4th century, and still the liturgical language of the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches and the Beta Israel.
Grown from the dialects of the Angles, Saxons and Jutes who settled in Britain, it became a language of government under Alfred the Great until the Norman Conquest.
The language of the Aztecs and of trade and empire across much of Mesoamerica, written after the Spanish conquest in the Latin alphabet, as in the Florentine Codex.
The Bantu speech of the East African merchant towns, rich in Arabic words from Indian Ocean trade, which caravans carried inland from Zanzibar in the 19th century.

title: Empires of the Sea
tagline: States whose power rested on fleets, ports and sea lanes, from Carthage to the British Empire.
intro: A thalassocracy is a state whose power rests on control of the sea, its trade routes and its ports rather than on large land territories. This path follows such powers from the ancient Mediterranean to the oceans of the modern world: Carthage and Athens, Srivijaya on the Strait of Malacca and the Chola navy that raided it, Venice on its lagoon, and the Portuguese, Dutch and British, who carried that kind of power across the oceans. Most were in the end worn down by rivals at sea or by powers on land.

steps.why: The term for a state built on the sea rather than on land, which needed less bureaucracy than a territorial empire; Srivijaya is the classic example.
A Phoenician colony of Tyre in Tunisia that built a trading empire across the western Mediterranean, until three Punic Wars stripped it of Sicily, Spain and its navy.
In 480 BCE the allied Greek fleet, led by Athens under Themistocles, defeated the larger fleet of Xerxes I in the straits off Attica, and Xerxes withdrew to Asia.
After Salamis the city led the Delian League, which it turned into a tribute-paying empire in the Aegean, until its defeat by Sparta in 404 BCE.
From Palembang in Sumatra it ruled the Strait of Malacca from the 7th to the 13th century, growing rich by taxing the shipping between China and India.
A Tamil dynasty of southern India that built a powerful navy, and whose raids on Srivijaya's ports in the 11th century weakened its hold on maritime trade.
A merchant republic on the lagoon whose fleets and colonies, from Dalmatia to Crete and Cyprus, made it the main link between Latin Europe and the East.
From Ceuta in 1415 a kingdom of perhaps a million people built the first sea-borne trading empire, opening the sea route to India with Vasco da Gama in 1498.
Its Baltic trade, its East India Company, founded in 1602, and the Amsterdam bank made it Europe's leading commercial power in the 17th century.
The Royal Navy's victory at Trafalgar in 1805 secured a century of naval supremacy for the largest empire in history, which dissolved within decades after 1947.

title: The Reformation and Its Wars
tagline: How Luther's protest of 1517 split Western Christianity and opened a century of religious wars.
intro: In 1517 Martin Luther wrote his Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences, and Western Christianity split into Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Anabaptist churches. Taken up or resisted by princes and cities, the new faiths became bound up with politics and war. This path follows the reformers, the Catholic answer of the Council of Trent, the settlements of Augsburg and Nantes and the wars around them, from the German Peasants' War to the Thirty Years' War, which the Peace of Westphalia ended in 1648.

steps.why: Begun by Luther's protest against indulgences in 1517, it taught salvation by grace through faith alone and broke the unity of Western Christianity.
The German monk whose Ninety-five Theses began the Reformation, who refused to recant before Charles V at Worms in 1521 and translated the Bible into German.
Partly inspired by the Reformation, peasants and townspeople rose in 1524–1525 demanding an end to serfdom; the princes' armies killed perhaps 100,000 people.
The French reformer whose Institutes became a founding text of Reformed Protestantism, and whose Geneva became a model and training centre for Reformed churches.
The Catholic answer: the Council of Trent (1545–1563) restated doctrine and reformed the clergy, while the Jesuits carried missions to the Americas and Asia.
Its fragmentation let the Reformation survive, and the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 let each ruler choose Catholicism or Lutheranism for his lands.
The killing of Huguenots in Paris and other French cities in 1572, during the French Wars of Religion, a year before Poland-Lithuania made religious tolerance law.
Henry IV ended the French Wars of Religion in 1598 by granting the Huguenots freedom of conscience and fortified towns; Louis XIV revoked it in 1685.
Beginning in 1618 as a religious struggle within the Holy Roman Empire, it widened into a contest among the major European powers and devastated much of Germany.
The treaties of 1648 that ended the war, confirmed the princes' power over religion in their lands, recognised Dutch independence and shaped the idea of territorial sovereignty.
